paragraphs: Crowdsourced labels are useful only if a learning system can account for workers making mistakes. This paper studies the error involved in recovering true labels from those unreliable responses. It starts from the observation that theoretical analyses of the widely used Dawid–Skene model have relied on restrictive assumptions about class frequencies, worker confusion patterns, or how many labels each worker supplies.

The authors derive a minimax error rate for a broader family of crowdsourcing models that includes Dawid–Skene. A minimax analysis characterizes the difficulty of estimation under the most challenging cases within the model family. Broadening that family makes the theory applicable to settings beyond those covered by earlier analyses.

The paper also introduces a worker clustering model and uses the new theory to investigate its behavior. Experiments show a strong resemblance between the theoretical lower bound and observed estimation error. That agreement connects the analysis to practical behavior, without asserting that empirical error always equals the bound.
icml-2018-analysis-of-minimax-error-rate.tldr: A broader minimax analysis of crowdsourced labeling supports a new worker clustering model and closely reflects observed estimation errors.

paragraphs: Representing an entire graph means turning its structure into features that another learning method can use. The paper distinguishes this goal from training a graph classifier directly. A supervised graph neural network learns representations around the labels supplied during training, whereas a task-independent representation is learned without organizing the embedding around a particular classification objective.

The authors build their approach around a graph object called an anonymous walk. They use this object to design unsupervised algorithms that learn whole-graph representations in both explicit and distributed forms. The contribution is therefore a way to construct reusable graph features, with scalability presented as a central property of the approach.

To evaluate the representations, the authors combine them with a support vector machine classifier. They report higher classification accuracy than the convolutional graph methods and traditional graph kernels considered. These results show that learning graph representations without task labels can still produce features that work well for downstream supervised classification.
icml-2018-anonymous-walk-embeddings-8f78.tldr: Anonymous walks support scalable, unsupervised whole-graph representations that improve classification accuracy in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Multiple instance learning handles examples that come as collections: a whole bag receives one label, while its individual instances do not receive separate labels. The paper models the probability of a binary bag label using neural networks. This makes the collection, rather than each item considered independently, the unit of supervised prediction.

Its main architectural contribution is an attention-based aggregation operator that combines information from the instances. The operator is permutation invariant, meaning that changing the order of items does not change the bag representation. Attention also provides insight into how individual instances contribute to the predicted bag label, making the aggregation useful for interpretation as well as prediction.

The reported results are comparable to the best methods on benchmark multiple instance learning datasets. The approach performs better than other methods on a dataset constructed from MNIST and on two histopathology datasets. These findings support the practical value of combining learned aggregation with instance-level interpretability, while distinguishing competitive benchmark performance from the stronger results on those particular datasets.
icml-2018-attention-based-deep-multiple-.tldr: Attention combines instances into an order-independent bag prediction while revealing their contributions and achieving strong empirical performance.

paragraphs: A black-box attack interacts with a classifier through its outputs rather than accessing the network directly. The paper argues that a common version of this setting gives attackers more access than practical systems often provide: unlimited queries and the complete output for every input. It studies whether attacks remain effective when that access is restricted.

The authors define three settings that separate different restrictions: limited numbers of queries, partial output information, and access only to predicted labels. They develop attacks for these conditions, targeting situations where earlier methods would be impractical or ineffective. The contribution is both a clearer account of attacker access and methods that work within those narrower interfaces.

Experiments demonstrate effectiveness against an ImageNet classifier under the proposed settings. The authors also report a targeted attack against Google Cloud Vision that handles limited queries, partial information, and practical complications. These demonstrations establish vulnerability in the evaluated systems despite restricted access; they do not require assuming that attackers can inspect every internal output.
icml-2018-black-box-adversarial-attacks-.tldr: The paper develops black-box adversarial attacks that remain effective under query limits, partial outputs, and label-only access.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation addresses the difficulty of using a model in an environment different from the one it learned from. This paper identifies complementary weaknesses in two approaches. Aligning internal features can overlook changes in pixels and low-level appearance, while translating images can neglect the higher-level meaning needed for the prediction task.

CyCADA combines alignment in image space with alignment in the model’s internal representation space. A discriminatively trained task guides the transfer, and consistency requirements preserve relevant semantics before and after adaptation. The purpose is to connect changes in visual appearance to the meaning that the downstream recognition system needs to retain.

The authors evaluate the approach on digit classification and road-scene semantic segmentation, among other visual settings. They report an advance over the state of the art for unsupervised adaptation from synthetic driving imagery to real driving environments. The finding supports the value of coordinating appearance and representation changes while keeping task-relevant semantics consistent throughout the transfer.
icml-2018-cycada-cycle-consistent-advers.tldr: CyCADA aligns images and internal features while preserving task semantics, improving unsupervised synthetic-to-real driving adaptation.

paragraphs: Ordinary backpropagation creates a dependency between layers during training: an earlier layer must wait for error information to travel backward from later layers. This backward locking limits how much updating can happen in parallel. The paper targets that dependency, especially in deep networks where previous attempts to remove it have suffered substantial performance degradation.

The proposed method divides a network into modules and uses delayed gradients to decouple their backward computations. This removes the locking between modules and makes parallel updates possible. The authors incorporate this mechanism into two stochastic optimization methods, connecting the parallel execution scheme to algorithms that can be analyzed mathematically.

For the nonconvex problem studied, they prove convergence to critical points. This is a convergence guarantee, not a claim that training always reaches a globally best solution. Experiments with deep convolutional networks on benchmark datasets support the analysis and show significant training speedups without accuracy loss in the reported evaluations.
icml-2018-decoupled-parallel-backpropaga.tldr: Delayed gradients enable parallel training across network modules, with critical-point convergence guarantees and reported speedups without accuracy loss.

paragraphs: The paper describes density modeling through invertible transformations that turn a structured probability distribution into a uniform one. It calls such a transformation a density destructor because it removes the original distribution’s structure. This perspective unifies earlier approaches, including Gaussianization and autoregressive density models, within a common mathematical interface.

A useful property is that the original density equals the absolute Jacobian determinant of its destructor. The determinant describes how the transformation locally changes volume, linking the transformation directly to probability density. This also connects shallow and deep models: each layer of a deep density model can itself be understood as a shallow density.

The framework is intended to make existing methods easier to combine, compare, and improve systematically. Using its connection to shallow densities, the authors introduce a destructor based on tree densities and another that uses pixel locality for images. They illustrate the framework on a two-dimensional dataset, MNIST, and CIFAR-10, presenting both a unifying viewpoint and concrete constructions.
icml-2018-deep-density-destructors-64ee2.tldr: Invertible transformations to a uniform density unify deep density models and motivate new tree-based and image-specific components.

paragraphs: An agent in a partially observed environment must act without seeing the complete state of the world. Its observations may also be noisy, and the environment’s dynamics may be unknown. This paper develops deep variational reinforcement learning to learn from that setting using the stream of observations and rewards available to the agent.

The method encourages the agent to learn a generative environment model and use inference within that model to combine available information. Instead of treating the observation history only as something to encode, it builds a latent state representation through model-based inference. The authors introduce an n-step approximation to the evidence lower bound so the environment model and policy can be trained jointly.

Joint training connects the learned representation to the control task, rather than leaving model learning separate from action selection. On Mountain Hike and flickering Atari, the approach outperforms previous methods that encode the past with recurrent neural networks. The evidence supports this combination of learned modeling, inference, and policy learning in the evaluated partially observed tasks.
icml-2018-deep-variational-reinforcement.tldr: DVRL jointly trains environment inference and a policy to improve decision-making from incomplete, noisy observations.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization uses gradient estimates, and reducing their variability can improve the behavior of optimization algorithms. This paper studies that idea for convex objectives made from finite sums, focusing on SVRG and its accelerated variant Katyusha. Its contribution is a shared analytical viewpoint for understanding their convergence and the role of acceleration.

The authors bring dissipativity theory from control into the analysis. Through an energy-conservation perspective, they express essential properties of these optimization methods using small semidefinite programs. This provides a route to automating convergence analysis with standard mathematical and computational tools, while also giving a physically motivated interpretation of algorithm behavior.

The framework recovers established convergence results for both SVRG and Katyusha and extends the analysis to alternative parameter choices. The authors also explain how it complements linear coupling, another technique for understanding acceleration. Together, these perspectives clarify accelerated variance reduction and offer a more systematic way to analyze related algorithms within the convex finite-sum setting.
icml-2018-dissipativity-theory-for-accel.tldr: Control-theoretic dissipativity yields a unified, partly automatable convergence analysis of SVRG and Katyusha through small semidefinite programs.

paragraphs: A classifier can perform poorly when deployment data follow a different distribution from its training data. Distributionally robust supervised learning tries to anticipate such shifts by optimizing against unfavorable alternatives. This paper examines a formulation based on f-divergences, which handles uncertainty by adversarially changing the weights assigned to training losses.

The authors prove a surprising result for the classification setting they analyze: this robust objective produces a classifier that fits the given training distribution exactly. Their explanation is excessive pessimism arising from two sources together—the classification losses and the breadth of distributions included in the robustness requirement. Merely optimizing a worst-case objective therefore does not deliver the anticipated response to shifted distributions in this analysis.

Motivated by that diagnosis, the authors propose a simple alternative DRSL approach designed to overcome the pessimism. Experiments demonstrate its effectiveness. The paper’s significance is the connection between the choice of loss, the range of allowed shifts, and the kind of classifier a robustness objective actually selects.
icml-2018-does-distributionally-robust-s.tldr: The analyzed f-divergence robust classification objective is overly pessimistic, motivating a simpler alternative with empirical support.

paragraphs: Robust Markov decision processes evaluate decisions while accounting for uncertainty represented by ambiguity sets. Their Bellman updates are a central computational step. This paper develops two exact algorithms that make those updates efficient for particular ambiguity-set structures, addressing the computation directly rather than replacing it with an approximate update.

The first algorithm uses homotopy continuation for L1-constrained state-action rectangular sets. It has quasi-linear running time for ordinary L1 norms and also extends to weighted L1 norms. The second uses bisection for state-rectangular sets; combined with the homotopy method, it also achieves quasi-linear runtime. Both return a primal solution as well as the optimal objective value, which supports their use in policy iteration.

Experiments report speedups of more than 1,000 times over Gurobi on small instances, with the gap increasing substantially as problems grow. These are empirical comparisons for the evaluated problems. Together with exactness and the runtime results, they show how exploiting the specified uncertainty structures can substantially reduce the cost of robust planning.
icml-2018-fast-bellman-updates-for-robus.tldr: Two exact algorithms accelerate robust Bellman updates for specified ambiguity sets and return solutions useful for policy iteration.

paragraphs: The paper studies nonconvex optimization problems with linear constraints using two algorithms: the Gradient Primal-Dual Algorithm and the Gradient Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers. Both use first-order information while updating primal and dual variables. The central question is whether these methods can reach the stronger target of second-order stationarity despite using only first-order information.

For the class of problems considered, the authors show that both algorithms reach second-order stationary solutions with probability one when the primal and dual variables are randomly initialized. The initialization condition is part of the result. Second-order stationarity is the stated target, so the guarantee should not be read as a claim of finding a global optimum.

The result extends earlier findings for algorithms that update primal variables alone. It also yields global convergence to second-order stationary solutions for two classes of unconstrained distributed nonconvex learning problems on multi-agent networks. This connects a constrained optimization theorem to learning systems whose computation is distributed across interacting agents.
icml-2018-gradient-primal-dual-algorithm.tldr: Under random primal-dual initialization, two first-order algorithms reach second-order stationary solutions almost surely for the studied problem classes.

paragraphs: Regression usually aims to predict a target value, but prior observations suggest that learning a distribution can improve prediction. This paper investigates why that can happen. It introduces a distributional regression loss and reports a significant improvement in prediction accuracy, extending the broader idea that softer targets can benefit supervised learning.

The authors examine explanations involving reduced overfitting and better learned representations. They instead find evidence supporting an optimization-based explanation: the proposed loss has better-behaved gradients and is easier to optimize. On this account, changing the training objective helps the learning process itself, and that improvement carries through to generalization.

To support the explanation theoretically, the paper characterizes the norms of the loss gradients. That analysis links the empirical findings to a concrete property of the objective rather than treating distributional prediction as an unexplained advantage. The result is evidence for a particular mechanism behind the observed gains, not a universal claim that every distributional regression loss improves every prediction problem.
icml-2018-improving-regression-performan.tldr: A new distributional regression loss improves prediction, with evidence pointing to easier optimization through better-behaved gradients.

paragraphs: Models with hidden binary variables can describe data generated by unobserved on-or-off factors, but estimating their parameters is computationally challenging, particularly with noise. This paper proposes a spectral method that learns from summary statistics of the observations. It uses eigenvectors associated with both a second-order moment matrix and a third-order moment tensor.

The approach extends earlier orthogonal tensor decomposition methods that assumed hidden units were statistically independent or mutually exclusive. Under mild non-degeneracy conditions, the authors prove consistent parameter estimation at the optimal parametric rate. Consistency means that the estimates approach the true parameters as data increase, with the stated conditions remaining essential to the guarantee.

The authors illustrate consistency using simulated data and demonstrate the method on a population-mixture model in genetics. These examples connect the mathematical result to both controlled data and an application. The contribution is a broader tensor-based learning approach whose statistical guarantees do not rely on the particular independence or exclusivity assumptions of the earlier methods.
icml-2018-learning-binary-latent-variabl.tldr: A moment-based spectral method learns binary latent-variable models consistently at the optimal parametric rate under mild non-degeneracy conditions.

paragraphs: The paper connects residual networks to boosting through a theory that combines improvements over features. Its multi-channel telescoping-sum construction leads to BoostResNet, a training algorithm that learns a sequence of shallow residual networks. The authors describe this sequential training as relatively inexpensive and particularly suitable for architectures containing nondifferentiable components.

The central guarantee depends on a weak learning condition: the module classifiers must perform slightly better than a specified weak baseline. When that condition holds, training error decreases exponentially with the number of trained blocks, or depth. The result explains how modest module-level performance can accumulate into a stronger network under the stated condition.

The authors also prove a generalization bound using margin theory. It suggests that residual networks with weights bounded in L1 norm could resist overfitting. That is a qualified implication of the bound, separate from the conditional training-error guarantee. Together, the results provide both a sequential training method and a theoretical account of when increasing depth can help.
icml-2018-learning-deep-resnet-blocks-se.tldr: BoostResNet trains shallow residual blocks sequentially and guarantees exponentially decreasing training error under a weak learning condition.

paragraphs: A hidden Markov model describes observations through hidden states, transition probabilities between those states, and emission probabilities for the observations. Learning these quantities can require long records, making expectation-maximization computationally prohibitive. This paper proposes an alternative suited to data that support reliable estimates of pairwise output probabilities but not higher-order statistics.

The authors show that pairwise co-occurrences can suffice to identify the model uniquely when the emission probabilities satisfy a sufficiently scattered condition. This is a conditional identifiability result: pairwise information is adequate for the stated class, rather than for every possible hidden Markov model. The algorithm uses that result to estimate transitions and emissions from observed data.

For topic modeling, the authors treat documents as observations from hidden Markov models that share the same topic emission probabilities. They report higher-quality topics than with a bag-of-words model. This application shows the potential value of modeling sequential structure while learning from pairwise statistics that can be estimated reliably.
icml-2018-learning-hidden-markov-models-.tldr: Pairwise emission statistics can uniquely identify an HMM under a sufficiently scattered emission condition, with benefits demonstrated in topic modeling.

paragraphs: Conventional differential-equation modeling begins with an equation for how a system changes and then estimates its coefficients. For complex systems, choosing that equation can be the main obstacle: the relevant interactions may be unknown. This paper moves the learning problem from estimating coefficients in a chosen equation to estimating the unknown dynamics themselves.

The authors use Gaussian process vector fields to learn nonlinear differential functions from observations of system states. These functions describe how the state changes over continuous time. The method retains the exact ordinary differential equation formalism while using a nonparametric representation, so the governing functional form does not need to be specified in advance.

The demonstrations show that the model can infer dynamics from sparse observations and simulate the system into the future. These capabilities connect learning the underlying rule of change with predicting a trajectory. The paper presents a broad modeling paradigm for unknown continuous-time dynamics, with empirical demonstrations of sparse-data inference and forward simulation.
icml-2018-learning-unknown-ode-models-wi.tldr: Gaussian process vector fields learn unknown continuous-time dynamics from state observations and support forward simulation within an ODE model.

paragraphs: Matrix sketching compresses a large matrix into a much smaller one while preserving information needed for later computation. This paper focuses on covariance error: how closely the sketch reproduces the original matrix’s product with its transpose in the specified orientation. The setting is streaming, allowing only one pass over the input and limited working memory.

Frequent Directions and its variants already achieve an optimal tradeoff between memory use and approximation error. The unresolved issue addressed here is speed. The authors introduce faster algorithms that preserve space optimality, improving running time without giving up the established relationship between storage and covariance accuracy.

They also give a conditional account of how much further runtime improvement is possible. Their algorithms are near-optimal unless the state-of-the-art time for matrix multiplication can be improved significantly. This ties the remaining computational room for progress to a broader matrix-computation problem, rather than claiming an unconditional lower bound that rules out all future improvements.
icml-2018-near-optimal-frequent-directio.tldr: Faster streaming matrix sketches retain optimal space-error tradeoffs and have conditionally near-optimal running times.

paragraphs: Autoregressive flows build probability models using invertible transformations whose individual steps depend on preceding variables. This paper generalizes the transformations used by Masked Autoregressive Flows and Inverse Autoregressive Flows. It replaces their conditionally affine single-variable transformations with a more flexible class represented by monotonic neural networks.

Monotonicity allows these richer transformations to remain invertible, preserving the defining structure of a flow. The authors show that neural autoregressive flows are universal approximators for continuous probability distributions. Their greater expressivity also helps capture multimodal targets, where probability mass concentrates around several different regions rather than a single dominant one.

Experiments report state-of-the-art results across a suite of density-estimation tasks. The method also outperforms Inverse Autoregressive Flows in variational autoencoders trained on binarized MNIST. These findings connect the stronger representational capacity to practical gains in the evaluated settings, while the universal approximation result concerns what the model class can represent rather than guaranteeing a particular training outcome.
icml-2018-neural-autoregressive-flows-b5.tldr: Monotonic neural transformations make autoregressive flows more expressive, with universal approximation capacity and strong density-estimation results.

paragraphs: Recurrent networks process sequences but can suffer when training gradients shrink or grow excessively. Orthogonal and unitary recurrent weights are approaches to this difficulty. This paper introduces scoRNN, a training scheme that maintains orthogonal recurrent matrices using real-valued parameters, with a straightforward gradient calculation and update.

The construction starts with a skew-symmetric matrix and maps it through the Cayley transform. That parametrization alone cannot represent matrices with an eigenvalue of negative one. The authors address this representational restriction by scaling the recurrent matrix with a diagonal matrix whose entries are positive or negative one. This scaling is a specific fix to the limitation of the unscaled parametrization.

In several experiments, scoRNN achieves better results with fewer trainable parameters than the other unitary recurrent networks compared. The findings support the proposed parametrization as a practical way to train orthogonal recurrent weights. The reported advantage applies to those experiments, rather than establishing superiority for every sequential learning task.
icml-2018-orthogonal-recurrent-neural-ne.tldr: A scaled Cayley parametrization maintains real orthogonal recurrent weights and achieves strong experimental results with fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Probabilistic programs offer a flexible way to express statistical models, but their structure can be difficult to exploit for efficient inference. In particular, useful independence relationships may be subtle. Graphical abstractions expose some distributional structure, yet the authors argue that graphs can be too coarse to capture properties that matter within programs.

Their alternative is to represent an abstraction as a simplified program. Keeping a program-shaped representation gives the framework another way to express structure relevant to decomposing inference. The authors provide a theoretical foundation for sound abstractions and an algorithm that generates them, connecting the representation choice to a principled construction procedure.

Experiments illustrate practical benefits when the framework is used to split probabilistic inference into components. The contribution therefore spans both formal reasoning and computational organization: simplified programs serve as abstractions that help expose opportunities for decomposition. The reported evidence illustrates the utility of this approach without asserting that every probabilistic program admits the same degree of simplification.
icml-2018-sound-abstraction-and-decompos.tldr: Sound abstractions expressed as simplified programs expose structure that can help decompose probabilistic inference.

paragraphs: A mixture model represents a distribution through a combination of component distributions. This paper considers one-dimensional mixtures whose components are unimodal, meaning each component has a single mode. It introduces a fully nonparametric and computationally efficient method, allowing generic unimodal components rather than requiring a specified parametric family for their shapes.

The method repeatedly perturbs an existing unimodal decomposition due to Baryshnikov and Ghrist. Through those perturbations, it produces a mixture described as optimal in topological and information-theoretic terms. The central idea is to use properties of unimodal decomposition to guide estimation, making the structure of the mixture part of the method itself.

The authors also address the case where the input consists directly of samples by developing a smoothing procedure. This procedure uses topological persistence of the unimodal category, connecting smoothing to how that structural quantity persists. Examples illustrate both the mixture-estimation method and the smoothing technique. The stated scope is one-dimensional mixtures with unimodal components.
icml-2018-topological-mixture-estimation.tldr: Topological mixture estimation uses unimodal decompositions and persistence-guided smoothing to estimate one-dimensional mixtures nonparametrically.

paragraphs: Predictive optimization chooses a decision by maximizing an objective estimated from data. The resulting best-looking decision can receive an overly optimistic evaluation: its estimated objective value exceeds its true value. This paper studies that optimism and develops corrections aimed at evaluating the selected solution more accurately.

The first correction resembles cross-validation. It removes the optimistic bias but goes too far in the opposite direction, underestimating the true objective value. This distinction matters because eliminating overestimation alone does not ensure an accurate evaluation. A correction can replace one systematic error with another.

The second approach, called parameter perturbation, uses resampling to address both directions of bias. The authors prove that it is asymptotically unbiased, meaning the bias vanishes in the relevant large-sample limit rather than necessarily being zero for every finite dataset. Experiments on artificial and real-world data show successful correction of optimism. The contribution concerns estimating the value of a data-selected decision more faithfully.
icml-2018-unbiased-objective-estimation-.tldr: Parameter perturbation uses resampling to correct optimistic evaluations in predictive optimization and achieves asymptotically unbiased estimation.

paragraphs: A reward function tells a reinforcement learning agent what outcomes to pursue, but its structure can also help organize learning. This paper introduces reward machines, finite-state machines that specify rewards while exposing their internal task structure. That representation supports dividing a larger learning problem into components.

The authors develop Q-Learning for Reward Machines, or QRM, which decomposes the machine and learns subpolicies for its components simultaneously through off-policy Q-learning. In the tabular setting, QRM is guaranteed to converge to an optimal policy. This distinguishes its stated guarantee from hierarchical reinforcement learning methods that may converge to suboptimal policies.

Experiments in two discrete domains demonstrate this behavior. The authors also incorporate function approximation, including neural networks, into QRM and show faster learning of better policies than hierarchical methods in a continuous-state domain. The optimality guarantee belongs to the tabular setting; the continuous-state result is empirical evidence that the structured approach can also be useful with function approximation.
icml-2018-using-reward-machines-for-high.tldr: Reward machines expose task structure for simultaneous subpolicy learning, with optimal-policy convergence guaranteed for tabular QRM.

paragraphs: Dropout has been interpreted as approximate Bayesian inference, giving a theoretical framework for analyzing and extending the training technique. This paper identifies mathematical problems in that interpretation. These include pathological or undefined posteriors arising from improper priors and a variational objective that becomes ill-defined when the approximating distribution is singular relative to the posterior.

The analysis suggests that the problems associated with the improper log-uniform prior in variational Gaussian dropout are generally irredeemable. The authors argue that the variational formulation suppresses some pathologies, explaining why the algorithm can still work. They separately address the singularity issue by proposing Quasi-KL divergence, an approximate inference objective for high-dimensional distributions.

The authors show that discretization- and noise-based motivations for variational Bernoulli dropout approach Quasi-KL as a limit. They also study its properties theoretically and through a simple Gaussian example: approximating a full-rank Gaussian with a degenerate one yields the principal component analysis solution. The proposed objective thus addresses a specific mathematical issue, rather than repairing every problem identified in Bayesian dropout.
icml-2018-variational-bayesian-dropout-p.tldr: The paper exposes flaws in Bayesian dropout interpretations and introduces Quasi-KL to address singular variational approximations.
